newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Britain's Blair edges Labour away from union roots.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Britain's Blair edges Labour away from union roots.

text.p: It had been a whirlwind nine months for Labour party members since Tony Blair became leader. But even they were stunned on April 29, 1995.

Blair had just pulled off a political coup, winning backing to ditch a clause in the party's constitution as sacred to traditional members as religious dogma -- the pledge of public ownership of key industries.
But then, as he stood to address delegates at the special conference called to endorse the change, he suddenly grinned.
"I want to say something about the party's name," he said. A nervous murmur ran round the hall. "It's staying as it is."
Relieved delegates laughed and cheered Blair's little joke, but behind the smiles lay a stark message.
Blair, who took over in July 1994 when John Smith died of a heart attack, was in charge -- and nothing would stand in his way in his desire to end Labour's 18 years in opposition.

Not content with ditching Clause Four, a battle which Labour leaders had been fighting on and off for over 35 years, Blair has left his mark on every part of the party machinery and revolutionised its internal democracy.
If he takes power after Britain's May 1 election, Blair will lead a party radically different to the bureaucratic, trade-union dominated Labour party which last ran the country in early 1979.
A recruitment drive and regular consultation of members -- not just the committed activists -- has revolutionised the annual conferences, once the bane of Labour leaders.
NEW LABOUR NEW POLICIES

Gone are the days when leaders were saddled by inconvenient policies. The influx of new members has meant the annual conferences are now an occasion for rubber-stamping of policies drawn up by Blair's team.
He constantly refers to the party as "New Labour" so maybe even a permanent name change may not be out of the question.

One relic of the old system remains. Under party rules, Blair will have to select his senior ministers -- after any election win -- from those voted onto the "shadow cabinet" list by Labour members of parliament before the election.
The list owes as much to deals between factions as to merit, and is not necessarily the one Blair would himself have chosen.
But the rules -- which Blair wants to change -- only bind the Labour leader for his first appointments, Labour officials say. As soon as he reshuffles his cabinet, his hands are no longer tied.
BIGGEST BATTLE AHEAD
By far the biggest battle ahead, and one Blair has only half completed, is a radical overhaul of Labour's links with unions.
Since it was born out of a desire for union representation at the turn of the century, Labour has always drawn the majority of its funds and its key activists from the unions.

But Blair himself has never made any secret of his desire to cut Labour's union links, arguing it is not right for a political organisation which could one day rule the country to be linked so closely to one special interest group.
Blair backed Smith's hard-fought battle at Labour's 1993 conference to trim union power.
Union leaders had traditionally wielded a "block" vote, representing members in their union, irrespective of their politicial affiliations or wishes.
This gave union barons huge powers over everything from the selection of election candidates to the choice of party leader and the formation of party policy.

After a cliffhanger vote, Smith's "one-member-one-vote" proposals won -- and local party members gained the power to choose their parliamentary candidates, individual union members won a say in party leadership elections and the unions' share of the vote at annual party conferences was cut to 70 percent.
Blair has gone further, cutting the union share of the vote to 50 percent, giving ordinary members an equal say.
This has allowed Blair to appeal directly to ordinary party members, most recently in his successful campaign for grassroots endorsement of Labour's pre-election manifesto.
SHIFT IN POLICY-MAKING POWER

As a result, the centre of policy-making power has shifted from the National Executive (NEC), Labour's powerful management committee once dominated by trade unionists and union-sponsored activists, to Blair's tightly controlled office.

Blair underlined this in January, pushing through changes to stop left-wing activists undermining a Labour government -- as in the 1960s and 1970s when ministers were shouted down at party conferences in the full glare of television cameras.
In a blow to the left-wing, who saw it as an attempt to stifle democracy, the NEC's policy-making role was downgraded.
The one all-powerful NEC will now be subordinate to the cabinet once Labour takes power, committed to supporting and promoting whatever policy the government decides.
The annual conference was also changed to make it more of a presentational body to celebrate party achievements rather than decide policy, again cutting the role of activists.
Blair has signalled he wants to go further.
CUTTING UNION TIES COMPLETELY

In a private briefing to parliamentary journalists at this year's party conference, Stephen Byers, a Labour employment spokesman, floated the idea that Labour was toying with the idea of cutting its links with unions altogether.
The outrage from the unions was deafening. But Byers, an MP close to Blair, survived without being disciplined, suggesting the idea is being seriously reviewed by Blair's team.
What is there to stop them? The final obstacle is funding.
But union funding has fallen. A decade ago, Labour took more than 77 percent of its 5.8 million pounds ($9.4 million) annual from unions.

By 1995, the union share had fallen to 54.2 percent of 12.5 million pounds. By next year, it could fall below the crucial 50 percent line. At the same time, individual membership -- and the number of private donors -- has soared.
Even corporate donors -- traditionally Conservative backers -- have started adding to Labour's coffers.
FUTURE FUNDING
But party funding is not the only destinaton for union funds. Unions make crucial donations to Labour's election fund and the campaign and office funds of individual MPs.
To replace such generosity would need more than just a surge in individual membership. Realistically, the only solution would be state funding of political parties.

State funding has been party policy for years, and the recent row about sleaze affecting former Conservative ministers, is likely to boost arguments in its favour. But getting it through parliament will be far from easy.
What Byers's unguarded comments suggest, though, is that Blair may be tempted to push such a move through if industrial unrest erupts during his term of office.

With the unions tamed and the party overhauled, there would be little left for him to change -- although Blair says change is not something he follows for its own sake but as a reaction to technological and social developments in the world.
One of his favourite catchphrases is that a party which does not change with the time "is not a movement, it's a monument". ($ = 0.614 British Pounds)
